extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and scholars of literature interested in Moby-Dick
extracted.subtask_description: Extract the evaluative and descriptive criteria critics use to analyze Herman Melville's Moby-Dick, covering narrative voice, structure, style, themes, symbolism, and sources. Useful for literary interpretation, teaching, or close reading of the novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view / Narrator (Ishmael)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ishmael is the narrator, shaping his story with many different genres; a distinction is made between Ishmael-as-narrator and Ishmael-as-character ('forecastle Ishmael'). Narrator Ishmael is called the novel's "central consciousness and narrative voice".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how first-person narration, the narrator's self-reflexivity (e.g., explicit remarks about writing), and the split between narrator and character affect reliability, perspective, and the novel's meditative digressions. Consider John Bryant's and Walter Bezanson's distinctions and resist one-to-one equation of Melville and Ishmael.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chapter structure (sequences, clusters, balancing chapters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapters can be divided into 'chapter sequences', 'chapter clusters', and 'balancing chapters'; sequences include narrative progression and thematic sequences (e.g., three chapters on whale painting), while clusters gather chapters on a shared theme (color white, meaning of fire).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the organization of chapters (narrative vs non-narrative), how 'events' (e.g., whale killings) provoke accompanying cetological essays and sermons, and how balancing chapters create oppositions or parallels (e.g., 'Loomings' vs 'Epilogue').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple genres and modes
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel uses many genres and modes including sermons, stage plays, soliloquies, songs, poetry, catalogs, stage directions, and emblematical readings; descriptions call the book 'encyclopedic' and 'variety of genres'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the effect of genre-mixing on tone, pacing, and thematic layering; note how shifts (e.g., from cetology to dramatic monologue) create contrasts and broaden the novel's scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural device: nine meetings (gams) with other ships
rubrics_metrics.description: A significant structural device is the series of nine meetings (gams) between the Pequod and other ships; these plot the rising curve of Ahab's passion and function as metaphysical parables, biblical analogues, or national pageants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze placement and interpretation of each gam: their contribution to narrative architecture, foreshadowing of fate, and how Ishmael reads each ship as an interpretable 'scroll'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Themes: epistemological quest and perception
rubrics_metrics.description: The hunt for the whale is read as a metaphor for an epistemological quest—man's search for meaning—and the novel emphasizes limitations of scientific knowledge and difficulty of perception ('All visible objects, man, are but pasteboard masks').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how cetological chapters, Ahab's monomania, and Ishmael's meditative stance dramatize tensions between knowledge, perception, and the 'ungraspable'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Themes: race and slavery
rubrics_metrics.description: Race is prominent (diverse crew, Queequeg and Pip) and the novel frequently mentions slavery; Pip's arc and racial dynamics (e.g., non-slavery context of Black characters) are central to thematic readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate representation of racial difference, Pip as the ship's conscience, and the novel's commentary on commodification and slavery (e.g., Pip compared to a fugitive slave advertisement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character contrast and double quest (Ahab vs Ishmael)
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrative is structured around two main characters—Ahab and Ishmael—intertwined and contrasted: Ahab as force of linearity/violence (monomania), Ishmael as digressive/meditative observer with a 'polypositional stance'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how characterization creates a bipolar observer/hero narrative and how each character's 'quest' (vengeance vs understanding) shapes thematic meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ahab's monomania and tragic heroism
rubrics_metrics.description: Ahab's obsession/monomania drives the plot and has been read as a tragic excess (Morbid over-ruling); critics compare him to Carlylean and Shakespearean heroic figures and discuss self-reliance pushed to solipsism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine Ahab's speeches, leadership over crew, prophetic interactions (e.g., Fedallah), and tragic consequences as evidence of heroic/diseased greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic, technical whaling detail (cetology and craft realism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed and realistic descriptions of sailing, whale hunting, and extracting whale oil and the rich cetological documentation are central features; cetology chapters function as encyclopedic documentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge how technical detail contributes to verisimilitude, thematic depth (limits of scientific knowledge), and the book's encyclopedic ambition; consider the two subpatterns of cetological documentation described in the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolism and emblematic objects (white whale, doubloon, coffin/buoy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols like the white whale, the doubloon nailed to the mast, and Queequeg's coffin (used as a buoy) carry layered meanings—each crew member reads the doubloon differently; Fedallah's prophecies and symbolic events (hearse/coffin imagery) are structurally important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how objects function as multi-voiced symbols, inviting varied interpretations (e.g., the doubloon as projection of personality) and how prophecies structure irony and fate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of foreshadowing and prophecy
rubrics_metrics.description: Fedallah's prophecies and narrative foreshadowing (e.g., fate of ships, typhoon as portent) are recurring devices that prepare and ironize the novel's tragic outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how prophecy shapes reader expectations, dramatic irony, and the fulfillment/ reversal of foretold events (e.g., two hearses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of stylistic registers and rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: Melville's language spans many registers—nautical, biblical, Homeric, Shakespearean, Miltonic, cetological, alliterative, fanciful, colloquial, archaic and allusive—and he blends high and low styles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate shifts among registers and how blending creates effects (e.g., comic prose poem passages, hymnic rhetoric), and how register differences index character and theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lexical innovation and word-formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Melville coins words, uses verbal nouns (plural), unusual adjectives/adverbs, participial adjectives/adverbs, rarities, and adjectival compounds to convey complex things; examples include 'allurings', 'uninterpenetratingly', 'teeth-tiered sharks'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how neologisms and unusual word formations contribute to voice, imagery, and the attempt to name the unnameable; consider Newton Arvin's analysis on 'Leviathanism' and part-of-speech play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and modification strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: The prose uses repetition and original modification of words (e.g., series like 'pitiable', 'pity', 'pitied') and other strategies such as using existing words in new ways and adopting specialized vocabulary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine cumulative rhetorical force produced by repetition and morphological play, and how it supports thematic emphasis or tonal modulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of simile—especially Homeric similes
rubrics_metrics.description: Melville employs elaborate Homeric similes with sustained, heroic dignity that both create dramatic movement and emphasize Ahab's hubris (e.g., land-images in chase scenes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate length, deployment, and cumulative effect of similes in heightening drama, producing breadth of imagination, and shaping reader perception in climactic passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical levels and composite blending
rubrics_metrics.description: Four rhetorical levels are identified: expository (cetological chapters), poetic (monologues that could be blank verse), idiomatic (character speech like Stubb's), and composite (blending of the others into passages of mixed register).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze which level predominates in given passages, how transitions function, and how composite passages achieve their distinctive effects (e.g., 'Nantucket' chapter as prose poem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assimilation of Shakespearean technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Melville's debt to Shakespeare is deep: dramatic diction, the use of verbs of action, blank-verse-like monologues, rhythmic control, verbal compounds, and a dramatic sense of language are singled out as catalytic to Melville's power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider Shakespearean echoes and techniques (e.g., use of dramatic verbs, rhythm, and 'making language itself dramatic') when evaluating speeches (Ahab) and tragic characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of Thomas Carlyle and other intellectual sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Parallels with Carlyle (Sartor Resartus, On Heroes) appear in rhetoric, emblematic universe ideas, and the Carlylean 'hero' model; critics note borrowings of metaphor and narrative strategy from Carlyle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for Carlylean concepts (emblematic universe, heroism) and other source influences when interpreting thematic and stylistic choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative architecture: ordering via 'events' and cetological essays
rubrics_metrics.description: Ten or more chapters on whale-killings function as 'events' that provoke chapter sequences or clusters of cetological lore; killings are structural occasions for ordering essays and sermons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how episodic whaling events interlock with digressive essays to build the book's architecture and thematic coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception vs discovery (semantic choices matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical attention to diction (e.g., Melville's change from 'discover' to 'perceive') highlights a theme: perception shapes what exists; perception is active and constitutive rather than mere finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine lexical nuances in translations/editions and how word choice reframes epistemological claims in passages of observation and revelation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of imagery and large-scale metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: Extended imagery welds crew, ship, and voyage into metaphors (e.g., 30 men becoming a single unit, ship as hull of contrasting materials unified by keel); imagery contributes 'startling energy' and dramatic focus on Ahab's will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how cumulative images and metaphors compress character relations, thematic aims, and the novel's tragic momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of moral and philosophical questions
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel explores class and social status, good and evil, and the existence of God; life-and-death of Ahab is read as critique of Emersonian self-reliance and as meditation on egoism and solipsism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how episodes, speeches, and symbolic events stage moral dilemmas and philosophical critiques rather than offering easy solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of the sea and setting as cultural space
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of life aboard ship, the diverse crew, and specific nautical places (Nantucket, Azores, Cape of Good Hope) function as both realistic backdrop and as a stage for cultural, social, and metaphysical encounters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider setting as active in shaping character dynamics and social commentary (e.g., racial mixing aboard Pequod, nautical labor practices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interplay of documentary voice and fictional artifice
rubrics_metrics.description: Ishmael's explanatory footnotes and the cetological apparatus establish a documentary genre aspect; critics call this a 'Nabokovian touch' and note the book's oscillation between document and drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the tension between factual-seeming documentation and imaginative fiction: how documentary elements bolster verisimilitude while also inviting metafictional reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readerly openness to multiple interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholars emphasize that Moby-Dick 'is full of meanings' and resists a single accounting; devices like the doubloon, ships, and varied registers invite polyvalent readings (metaphysical parable, biblical analogue, national allegory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how textual ambiguity and polysemy are deliberate features that demand interpretive plurality rather than definitive closure.
